bindingDocumentation: Two questions, two axes. `category` answers why a canonical route exists and which part of the projection it belongs to. `binding` answers whether Rust binds it and, when it does not, why not -- with evidence, and with a durable task when the reason is temporary. A purpose is never an answer to the binding question: 'this backs XNA' says nothing about whether the Rust projection reaches it. BOUND is measured from the reviewed cna-sys slice and is never declared here; every other status must be stated, and every statement must carry a reason and evidence a reader can check.

knownDefects.summary: a content-loaded Model's teardown faults: ~MeshResource moves an empty detachedValue over a loaded part's value, and ~PartResource dereferences it. Every route answers correctly; only teardown is affected, and leaking the handle moves the fault to process exit rather than avoiding it. The routes stay BOUND because they work -- this records the defect against them so the scoreboard is not the only thing a reader sees.

refuses a skin the content pipeline imported -- 'The Model skin's skeleton was not created through the C API' -- which is not the refusal the header documents. The route is bound and works for a skin added through cna_model_add_skin_ext.

rules.reason: both answer a CNA_ObjectDictionaryHandle or a foreign object made by a caller's own reflective reader, and neither the ObjectDictionary projection nor the reflective type-reader builder exists in Rust yet. Both belong to the content slice, so these two go with it rather than dragging fifteen content_readers.h routes into the models slice to reach them.
rules.evidence: content_readers.h's cna_object_dictionary_* and cna_reflective_type_reader_* families, all still unbound

rules.reason: cna_camera_create_with_test_backend_ext points CNA's global platform override at memory the camera handle owns, and cna_camera_destroy frees it without clearing the override, so any later camera query reads freed memory. Measured as SIGSEGV (wait status 139) from Rust; the baseline sequence without that query exits 0. Building a projection on a lifecycle that faults would mean hiding it.

these build a native Model by hand, and crates/cna/src/graphics/model.rs already is the XNA Model in Rust: Model, ModelBone, ModelMesh, ModelMeshPart, their collections and enumerators, CopyAbsoluteBoneTransformsTo and Draw, built by this crate's own .xnb ModelReader and disposed through ContentDisposable. Binding these would put a second, weaker Model in the crate -- one whose parts are opaque handles rather than typed Rust values -- for callers who already have the real one. The read side of the same header is bound, because a model CNA loaded carries glTF facts the Rust reader cannot produce.

this tag is an opaque 64-bit slot for a C caller's own pointer -- upstream calls it 'the C-owned opaque model tag' and never reads it. A Rust caller attaches data by keeping it in their own type, which is typed, borrow-checked and cannot outlive what it describes. The tag an asset actually carries is a different route, cna_model_get_content_tag_dictionary_ext, and that one is tracked rather than refused.
rules.evidence: models.h's own contrast between cna_model_get_tag and cna_model_get_content_tag_dictionary_ext: 'That one is a C-owned opaque value a caller sets and reads back; this one is what a custom ContentProcessor wrote into the .xnb'

rules.reason: XNA's ToString() formats, which Rust implements for each of these types with the same layout: Viewport::ToString, GamePadState::ToString, MouseState::ToString, TouchLocation::ToString, and the five sensor readings plus the legacy AccelerometerReadingEvent. Named one by one rather than by suffix on purpose -- the same routes exist for types Rust has no ToString for yet, and a wildcard here would quietly claim a fidelity this crate does not have.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/graphics/viewport.rs, crates/cna/src/input/gamepad.rs, crates/cna/src/input/mouse.rs, crates/cna/src/input/touch.rs, crates/cna/src/extensions/sensors.rs; each format was read off the matching cnanext ToString() rather than guessed

rules.reason: these are pure value arithmetic, and cna::value implements each operation in Rust: Matrix::Invert, CreateLookAt and Decompose, Vector3::Normalize, Quaternion::Slerp, BoundingBox::Intersects, BoundingFrustum::Contains and Color::FromNonPremultiplied are Rust functions over Rust values. Binding the C route would put a second implementation of the same arithmetic behind a native call that can fail, and the two could disagree.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/value/, and crates/cna/src/value/tests.rs which measures the Rust arithmetic against XNA's documented results

rules.reason: XNA's Equals and GetHashCode exist because a .NET value type inherits object. Every Rust counterpart of these types derives PartialEq -- GamePadState, MouseState, KeyboardState, DisplayMode, SensorInfo, JoystickInfo, the sensor readings -- so `a == b` is the operation, the compiler checks it, and a HashMap key works without asking C anything. Where XNA's named methods matter for source fidelity the Rust types carry them too. Binding these would add a fallible native call that answers a question `==` has already answered, and the two could disagree.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/input/gamepad.rs, crates/cna/src/input/mod.rs, crates/cna/src/input/mouse.rs, crates/cna/src/input/touch.rs, crates/cna/src/extensions/sensors.rs -- every type these routes name derives PartialEq, and TouchLocation, KeyboardState and the GamePad* types also spell XNA's own Equals and GetHashCode

rules.reason: these are XNA's constructors reached through C: cna_viewport_init is ToC(Viewport()) and cna_gamepad_state_init_from_values is the parameterised constructor. Rust builds these values with Default, a `new`, or a struct literal, none of which can fail. The descriptor structs that carry struct_size and struct_version are filled at the call site with size_of and the version the header states, and tools/native-abi/verify.py probes every layout against the headers -- so the field-setting these routes exist to get right is already checked by a stronger mechanism than a runtime call.
rules.evidence: crates/cna/src/graphics/viewport.rs, crates/cna/src/input/gamepad.rs, crates/cna/src/graphics/presentation.rs; tools/native-abi/verify.py's layoutTypesProbed, which checks every descriptor's field order and offsets against the canonical headers

rules.reason: these answer .NET's GetType().Name, and upstream's implementations are all compile-time constants -- every GetTypeName() in cnanext returns a fixed string such as 'Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Input.KeyboardState'. A Rust caller knows the type statically at every call site, so there is no reflection question to ask, and the .NET name of a Rust value is not a fact about that value. The one place these strings genuinely matter is the content format, where the reader name is part of the .xnb, and the crate already carries them as data in AssetTypeId rather than fetching them one object at a time.
rules.evidence: cnanext modules/*/src/Xna/*.cpp -- every GetTypeName() is a constant; crates/cna/src/content/reader.rs, which names the canonical readers directly
